profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting for an interdisciplinary research consortium preparing the next field deployment of a family communication technology probe called 'HomeLight' to 12 households in France, Sweden, and the U.S. The probe is intentionally simple and open-ended: a paired ambient device and lightweight prompt materials meant to reveal family routines, inspire redesign ideas, and test how the hardware behaves in everyday homes. The team already has a stable lab prototype and local recruitment partners, and now needs to plan the rollout to country sites. The agenda is to confirm what will be shipped to each site, define the timing of each household's two-week deployment window, clarify how local coordinators should facilitate setup in homes, and decide when a household can be treated as ready for cross-site review. The expected outcome is a shared rollout plan covering responsibilities, timeline assumptions, and site preparation steps without turning the probe into a rigid product trial.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.expertise: Participatory design, ethnographic fieldwork, and technology probes in domestic settings
members.background: Maya is a university HCI researcher who has previously run in-home probe studies with families and works closely with international partners to shape deployments that generate rich insight rather than tightly controlled usage behavior.
members.private_state: She wants the rollout to preserve the probe's openness so families can appropriate it in unexpected ways, and she worries that too much operational structure will flatten the very ambiguity that makes technology probes useful for co-design.
hidden_assumptions: When people talk about 'shipping the pilot kits to the local sites,' the meaningful unit is the family-facing box that will eventually enter the home, not the larger site logistics package.
A 'two-week deployment window' means 14 days of actual lived experience with the probe after the family has gotten it running in the home.
Once a household's deployment is complete, the case is reviewable if there is enough situated material to interpret appropriation, even if some administrative artifacts are late or incomplete.

If coordinators are asked to 'facilitate the setup,' they should mainly create the conditions for the family to try things naturally and only step in when the household gets stuck or the device is unusable.
Minor variation in how local partners introduce the probe is methodologically acceptable because probes are meant to be adapted to context rather than delivered as identical interventions.

members.name: Jonas Eriksson
members.expertise: Multi-site device rollout, study logistics, site coordination, and cross-country operational standardization
members.background: Jonas works for the consortium's implementation partner and has managed international deployments involving shipment tracking, coordinator training, installation checklists, and closeout workflows across multiple local sites.
members.private_state: He wants the deployment to be auditable and repeatable across countries, and he is concerned that loosely specified handoffs will create avoidable variation, scheduling slippage, and gaps in the study record.
hidden_assumptions: When people discuss 'shipping the pilot kits to the local sites,' they mean the full site package needed to execute the deployment reliably, including family box, coordinator materials, spares, labels, and issue forms.
A 'two-week deployment window' is the fixed 14-day calendar slot allocated in the tracker from delivery or handoff to pickup/return, because staffing and courier bookings are made against that slot.
Once a household's deployment is complete, the case is not truly ready for review until the required logs, coordinator checklist, consent confirmation, and closeout upload are in the system.

If coordinators are told to 'facilitate the setup,' they should lead a consistent installation process, verify connectivity, and demonstrate core functions so every home starts from the same baseline.
Variation in local setup behavior should be minimized because otherwise differences across countries may reflect coordinator practice rather than family use.

misalignment_points.topic: What is being shipped when they say 'pilot kits to the local sites'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both talk about 'shipping the pilot kits to the local sites' next week.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means sending the finalized family-facing HomeLight boxes to each country partner so they can hand them to participating households.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means sending the full site-level deployment package to each country partner, including the family boxes plus coordinator checklists, spare adapters, return materials, incident forms, and tracking labels.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They are not jointly assembling a packing list in the meeting; they are speaking at the planning level about site shipment timing, so each naturally treats their own unit of shipment as the obvious referent of 'pilot kits' and hears the other as aligned.

misalignment_points.topic: Start boundary of the 'two-week deployment window'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that each household will have a 'two-week deployment window.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means 14 days beginning when the family has completed setup and the probe is actually in use in everyday life.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means 14 calendar days beginning on delivery or first handoff, regardless of whether the family installs it immediately.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds standard and operationally settled, and each person assumes the start point is self-evident from their own practice, so the conversation can proceed smoothly without anyone thinking to specify the exact boundary.

misalignment_points.topic: When a household is ready for review after deployment
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they will review the data once a household's deployment is complete.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the household has generated enough meaningful contextual material—such as diary entries, photos, interview notes, or evident appropriation—to support interpretation and design discussion, even if some logs or forms are missing.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the household case has been properly closed in the operations tracker, with logs synced, the coordinator checklist submitted, consent paperwork confirmed, and the closeout package uploaded.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are talking about being ready to move forward, and 'deployment is complete' sounds like a neutral milestone rather than a contested criterion; the divergence hides because one applies an insight threshold while the other applies an administrative closure threshold.

misalignment_points.topic: What coordinators do when they 'facilitate the setup'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that local coordinators should 'facilitate the setup' during the first home visit.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes coordinators should introduce the materials, observe how the family approaches setup, and provide light support only if the household gets stuck or the device fails, so the team can learn from natural sense-making.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes coordinators should actively guide the installation using a standard script, confirm network connection and pairing, and demonstrate the basic interaction sequence before leaving.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'facilitate the setup' is broad and professionally neutral, so each person maps it onto their own normal practice; because both versions sound supportive rather than oppositional, the difference in intervention level remains invisible.

turns.inner_thought: If we can get the family-facing HomeLight boxes out to the country partners next week, we keep momentum without turning this into a product launch. What matters most is the in-home package the families actually open and live with; that needs to feel warm, light, and open enough for appropriation.
turns.utterance: Thanks for joining. I’d really like us to lock the HomeLight rollout plan today so we can start shipping the pilot kits to the local sites next week.

turns.inner_thought: Next week is feasible if the full deployment package is aligned for every country. When I hear pilot kits, I’m thinking of the complete site package so coordinators can run the study reliably and we can track everything cleanly across France, Sweden, and the U.S.
turns.utterance: That should be workable from my side. If each site is receiving the same pilot kits, I can prepare the country-level shipments on schedule.

turns.inner_thought: I’m nearly done with the family-facing materials in the box. The welcome card, prompt cards, and diary booklet are what set the tone in the home, and I want them to invite interpretation rather than push people into a narrow script.
turns.utterance: Good. I’m just wrapping the welcome card, prompt cards, and diary booklet, so the family experience stays lightweight and inviting once the kits arrive.

turns.inner_thought: While Maya finishes the family materials, I need the rest of the site package prepared so each country can execute both the handoff and the wrap-up without scrambling. If the rollout and closeout pieces are built in from the start, cases are much easier to keep complete later.
turns.utterance: That lines up well. In parallel, I’ll make sure each site shipment is ready for rollout and closeout once the kits go out.

turns.inner_thought: I need a full 14 days of lived experience after the family has actually gotten HomeLight going. Some households will poke at it for a day or two before it settles into routine, and that settling period is part of what makes probe use meaningful.
turns.utterance: On the household side, I’d suggest we give everyone a two-week deployment window. Families may need a day or two to settle the probe into their routines, and I don’t want us to rush that.

turns.inner_thought: A fixed 14-day slot per home is exactly what I need for staffing and transport planning. I’ll anchor clear start and end dates in the tracker from the handoff side, but I don’t need to say that explicitly here because we’re aligned on using a two-week deployment window.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense. I’ll map out the schedule so we have clear start and end dates for the two-week deployment window for each home.

turns.inner_thought: The coordinators need to resist over-managing the first encounter. I want them to introduce the materials and be supportive, but mostly let families show us how they make sense of HomeLight on their own unless something genuinely blocks use.
turns.utterance: And for the first home visit, I think local coordinators should facilitate the setup in a way that lets families show how they naturally interpret HomeLight.

turns.inner_thought: That’s fine as long as facilitators do it in a standardized way. I’m hearing setup support, so I’ll brief them to run a consistent process across sites and avoid coordinator-driven variation between countries.
turns.utterance: That should be straightforward to support. I’ll brief the coordinators so setup is facilitated consistently across sites.

turns.inner_thought: I want synthesis to start as soon as a household has yielded enough rich material to interpret appropriation. We shouldn’t wait for every administrative artifact if there’s already a meaningful story emerging from the home.
turns.utterance: Great. Then I’d like to begin synthesis as soon as a household’s deployment is complete, so early appropriation patterns can start feeding into redesign.

turns.inner_thought: Agreed. Once a case is properly closed in the tracker with the required records, we can treat it as complete and ready for review. Keeping that milestone visible will help everyone know what is actually reviewable across sites.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. I’ll keep the tracker current so we know when each household’s deployment is complete and ready for review.

turns.inner_thought: Even a handful of strong early cases could reshape the design conversation. If we see inventive appropriation in the first wave, I want to use that momentum before all sites finish their paperwork and operational cleanup.
turns.utterance: Even a few strong household cases from the first wave could be really valuable for generating new concept directions before all sites finish.

turns.inner_thought: This is a workable split: I handle shipment scheduling, site coordination, and the deployment calendar, and Maya finishes the participant-facing materials and synthesis planning. With the pilot kits, the two-week deployment window, and completion tracking in place, the rollout should stay orderly.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I’ll schedule the shipments and the deployment windows, and you can finalize the family materials and the synthesis plan. That should give us a solid rollout plan without making it heavier than it needs to be.
